Hi, yeah... thanks. Um, so, I guess I came in because... well, it’s actually my eating, it just went completely off the rails recently. And you have to understand, I’m a project manager, so my whole life is usually organized down to the minute. I have spreadsheets for everything. I usually track all my meals, my macros, the whole nine yards. I'm very meticulous about it. 

But lately... I don't know, I just completely stopped caring about my food tracking. Like, I didn't even open the app. I just threw the whole routine out the window. I ended up skipping real meals for days at a time. Literally days. I was just living on black coffee and whatever chalky protein bars I could dig out of the bottom of my briefcase, and even then I was only eating them because they were right there in front of me. I didn't even feel like I needed real food. I didn't even notice what it was doing to my body, honestly, until a couple of days ago when I put on my work trousers and they were just... hanging loose. Like, really loose, bunching up at the waist. I had to pull my belt two notches tighter just to keep them from falling down, and it really threw me because I hadn't even noticed I was shrinking. I just hadn't noticed at all. So, yeah, the fact that I'm just sort of fading away without realizing it... that's why I'm here.

Yeah... yeah, actually, it’s not just the food. It’s pretty much everything else, too. I haven't wanted to hike, edit photos, log my meals, or even touch the woodworking project I have set up in my garage. And that’s really strange for me, because those things usually keep me grounded.

It’s like the cord just got unplugged. Normally, having those projects, having those steps—step A to step B to step C—that’s what anchors me. Whether it's weighing my food or sanding a piece of walnut, that structure is what keeps my head on straight. But right now, the thought of doing any of it just feels completely impossible, or just... pointless, I guess? I don't know, it's just bizarre to look at all these tools and hobbies that usually define my weekends and just feel completely blank about them.

Well, honestly, I don't know the exact number because, like I said, I stopped weighing myself. Well, it... honestly, it was exactly at the same time. Right when that crushing sadness hit me after that awful presentation. I think I mentioned earlier that I usually track my meals? I mean, I was the guy who weighed his chicken breast on a digital kitchen scale to the exact gram and logged every single macronutrient into an app. I had my daily intake calculated down to a science. I had to force myself to take a bite just so I wouldn't pass out while staring blankly at my monitor. The thought of actually cooking, or even just ordering a sandwich, felt like climbing a mountain. 

And it’s crazy because I didn't even notice the physical changes at first. I was just so trapped in this fog of feeling completely worthless that I wasn't paying attention to my own body. But then, maybe a few weeks into this whole ordeal, I put on my favorite pair of work slacks—these charcoal grey trousers I had custom-tailored because I’m usually very particular about how my clothes fit—and they were just hanging loose on me. They were practically bagging at the knees. I had to pull my belt two whole notches tighter than normal just to keep them up. I had lost all this weight without even trying, without even noticing it was happening, just because the sadness completely wiped out any desire I had to put food in my body. So, yes, the depression and the eating changes... they were completely intertwined from day one.

Well, that's... that's a really interesting question, actually. Because I've thought about that. I've thought about it a lot, lying there on the couch, staring at the popcorn ceiling—which, by the way, is a terrible design choice, I keep meaning to scrape it off, but obviously I haven't had the energy for that either. But I've wondered, you know? If I just forced myself to go into the garage and pick up a piece of sandpaper, or if I just made myself lace up my hiking boots and drive to the trailhead... would it flip a switch? Would it jump-start the system?

Because in project management, right, sometimes you have a dependency that's holding everything up. And if you can just clear that one blocker, the rest of the workflow starts moving again. So I’ve analyzed it from that perspective. Like, is the lack of hobbies the blocker, or is the sadness the blocker? 

And honestly? I just... I don't know. I really don't. Because it feels like a chicken-and-egg situation. The sadness is so heavy, so all-consuming, that it feels like it's the root cause of why I can't do the hobbies. But then, without the hobbies—without the woodworking, without the hiking, without that methodical, tangible progress that I can measure and see—I don't have any way to pull myself out of the sadness. It's like a feedback loop. A negative feedback loop.

Honestly, like I was explaining earlier... that whole situation is actually the main reason I even came in here to see you today. Because my eating just went completely off the rails.
